title: 1 Samuel 11:12–15
context: 1 Samuel 11:12–15 follows the victory. The people want to execute those who had despised Saul (10:27), but Saul refuses because the LORD has rescued Israel that day. Samuel leads the people to Gilgal to renew the kingdom, and they make Saul king before the LORD with peace offerings and great rejoicing. Both traditions see Saul at his best here, generous in victory and crediting the LORD, and both note that the kingdom is renewed in a setting of worship.

verses.text: The people said to Samuel, “Who is he who said, ‘Shall Saul reign over us?’ Bring those men, that we may put them to death!”
verses.arminianNotes: The people ask Samuel to bring out the men who had asked, "Shall Saul reign over us?" so that they may be put to death. Arminian readers see the danger of turning victory into vengeance, and note that the people’s enthusiasm needed restraint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and connect the request with the worthless men of 10:27 who despised Saul. Both traditions read the verse as testing how Saul will use his new popularity and power.

verses.text: Saul said, “No man shall be put to death today; for today the LORD has rescued Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul refuses: no one will die today, because the LORD has rescued Israel. Arminians see Saul at his best, showing mercy and giving God the credit, a model of humble leadership that Saul would later fail to sustain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that Saul’s restraint flows from recognizing that the deliverance belongs to the LORD. Both traditions see the verse as a high point in Saul’s reign and read the rest of his story in contrast with it.

verses.text: Then Samuel said to the people, “Come! Let’s go to Gilgal, and renew the kingdom there.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel calls the people to go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there. Arminian readers see the renewal as a public commitment by the people to the king God had chosen, sealed after the victory has confirmed him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Interpreters discuss how this renewal relates to Saul’s earlier anointing (10:1) and public selection (10:24). Both traditions read Gilgal, with its history in Joshua 4–5, as a fitting place to renew covenant commitment.

verses.text: All the people went to Gilgal; and there they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal. There they offered sacrifices of peace offerings before the LORD; and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
verses.arminianNotes: At Gilgal they make Saul king before the LORD, offer peace offerings, and rejoice greatly. Arminians see joyful worship marking the beginning of the monarchy, with the people’s choice made before the LORD rather than apart from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress the phrase "before the LORD," which places the kingship under God’s authority. Both traditions note that the joy of this verse is followed immediately by Samuel’s sober warning in chapter 12.
